utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution calls Colonel Jacques Morneau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. No protective measures, I take it from --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Morneau. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. [Interpretation] Did you decide to testify in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, we will continue in English. [In English] Mr. Morneau, you'll first be examined by Ms. Mahindaratne, who is counsel for the Prosecution. I add to that that I address you as Mr. Morneau. That is not because of any disrespect for your military rank, but since in this Chamber we address persons, individuals, as -- in their primary capacity as persons coming to tell us the truth, and therefore military ranks are as such not of any importance. Don't understand it as any disrespect. And others might choose to do otherwise. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Morneau.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Colonel Jacques Morneau.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you provide three statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, the first one being on 26th and 27th August, 1996; the second one on 25th November, 2003; and the third one on 25th February 2008?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday did you have the opportunity to examine all three statements?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you find the contents of those statements, that the contents accurately reflected what you had stated to the members of the Office of the Prosecutor on those three occasions?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document 5159, please, on the screen. Colonel, are the contents of your statements, all three statements, true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you were asked the questions that were asked of you by the members of the Office of the Prosecutor on those three occasions today in court, would your responses be the same as those reflected in your three statements?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel, would you please look at the screen in front of you. Is that your statement of 26th and 27th August, 1996. And if you could just move to the signature page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, from written submissions the Chamber understands that there are no objections from any party. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P308.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P308 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I call for document number 5160, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, there will be another document coming up on your screen. If you could identify that this is your statement of 25th November 2003 for the record.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to the signature page. Mr. President, may I tender this statement in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I make the same observation as in relation to the previous document. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P309, the November 2003 statement of the witness is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can I call for document number 5161 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Colonel Morneau, you'll have the third statement also coming up on your screen. If you could identify that it is your statement of 25th February 2008.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the document could be given a P number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same observation as in relation to the two previous documents, that is, no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P310, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P310 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, at the time you made the supplementary statement, that is the third one, on 25th February 2008, did you examine a number of documents, most of which were reports submitted to you by CanBat personnel on their observations during Operation Storm and its aftermath?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At the same time did you also examine some photographs and a sketch map?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you have the opportunity to look at those documents yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that the contents of those documents are accurate and true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, five documents, a set of photographs and a sketched map was tendered by the 92 ter summary -- I beg your pardon, 92 ter submission. If they could be given a sequential P numbering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have to go through it step by step. There were two documents which were not yet on your 65 ter list, although you announced initially that it would be four but then you reported that two of them were mentioned by mistake. The Defence submissions make clear that there's no objection against adding the 65 ter -- the two documents which were not yet on the 65 ter list, to add them to the 65 ter list. Therefore, that request as we find it in your 92 ter motion is granted. Now we come to the next step, that is whether there are any objections against the documents. Perhaps we go through them one by one. If you would first -- mention the first one, we'll invite Mr. Registrar. We'll then ask the Defence whether there's any objection. We'll invite Mr. Registrar to assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very good, Mr. President. May I call for document number 167, please. Mr. President, I have a couple of questions with regard to these documents. To save time should I also take the opportunity then, since the document is up on the screen, to ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that saves time in getting it off the screen and getting it on the screen again. But let's first look at 65 ter 167. Any objections? No objections. Then, Mr. Registrar, that would be number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P311, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P311 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Mahindaratne, if you want to put questions to the witness, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, is this a report submitted to you by CanBat personnel?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you state as to who compiled this report?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: That was my section of military information within the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what is the manner or what is the basis on which the data reported in this report was collected?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, within the battalion we do reports at all levels, at the observation post level they log their own information, at the company levels they log their own information, at the battalion headquarter level they log their own information. As part of the function of that military information section is to collect that information and try to make sense of the information they gather from all the different sources within the battalion and then they produce reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how do you ensure that the contents or the data reported in these reports are accurate?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, within the battalion structure, I mean we have the -- that section of the military information section, and that is they report -- normally the ops officer was a second source to -- would double-check the work of that section and also the company commander of that support company verified information. And within the battalion itself, myself I come across a number of facts or evidence or information that talking or visiting my companies so I can cross-check some of that information when they send a report to, if it makes sense to me or not then I can assess that, yes, that the information is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this report was submitted to you in the course of ordinary course of business or did you specifically order your subordinate personnel to submit this report to you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I asked following the offensive operations that we witnessed in the beginning of August to make up a report to I will say register what happened because memories fade away quickly and the writing stays. So I asked the officers to put down on paper what their recollection of the incidents that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What did you do with this report?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, that was a report that we used to inform our superior headquarters, at the sector headquarters and also on the national level, I mean we had to inform our own nationalities about what happened in this event because as a Canadian military organization we have what we call a war diaries and we have information that we have to produce for our own archives in Canada to register the actions of the Canadian soldiers in operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So are you saying you submitted or forwarded this report onwards to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 313, please. Mr. President, may I ask the questions before it's admitted into evidence, because I had put this document into context before it's admitted into evidence. May I ask a couple of questions from the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, this document doesn't have a heading and it looks as if it's a continuation of another document. Is it correct to say that this is a continuation of the previous document, P311?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may it be given a P number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections -- I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P312.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P312 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, could you please turn to paragraph 30, look at paragraph 30 of this document and on the screen if we could have page 3, on the B/C/S version also it's the same page. Next page, actually, I'm sorry, it should be page 4. It should be -- we should go on to paragraph 30. Thank you. There's a report here, Colonel, that following the operation, specialised units were seen wearing black Balaclavas and that they were seen going from house to house in mop-up operations. And it's also recorded during this period afterwards not allowed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. Excuse me, Colonel. It doesn't say they saw that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When such objections are raised you're invited to quote literally from what the document says. Apart from that, Ms. Mahindaratne, I do not see any B/C/S version of this document uploaded on the system.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was from the previous one, so you say this is the continuation of the previous document. Where is the continuation of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's a good question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- find it. Once you find it, take care that it's uploaded and if the Defence have any problems with it, practical problems, then they're invited to advised me. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It says -- let me read it to you and perhaps you can read it to yourself, Colonel. "Following the success of the units at the front, specialised units wearing black Balaclavas went from house to house to mop up. During this period, our troops were not allowed to patrol the sectors. We suspect that civilians were quite simply killed." Now, Colonel, do you recall that particular report?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I recall that report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the reference to black Balaclavas, is it something like a ski mask covering the face?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: That's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you recall what was reported to you on this matter?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: On this matter -- I mean, again that military section, when they do prepare that report they collect information from all the different sources they can have. And like I said, they went and consulted and interviewed also the people in the different companies throughout the battalion, and when they make up their report some of the elements of the battalion reported that they saw that kind of units at the front lines of the troops, that they were going and searching houses and they were covered with Balaclavas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you informed as to, when you say units, what forces these units belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: When I unit or subunit it is part of the different companies within the battalion or platoons or OPs, I mean the intelligence section. When they do their work I mean they are always in constant communications with different element of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel, I think you misunderstood my question. I was referring to the specialised units which was seen moving - I'm sorry, I withdraw the word - just reported to be moving from house to house wearing Balaclavas. Now, did you have information as to which forces these units belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: What it was not a specific unit but they were reported as being special force, special force following the front -- the front units, that they were special units especially for those specific tasks of clearing out houses after the front troops have passed through the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When I say "units," I'm not asking for you to identify what units they were. I'm asking -- when I use the word which forces, is it the military or the Ministry of the Interior or some other form of forces?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: It was a Croat army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, if we ask for some clarification on the actual unit that they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has stated that he can't identify the unit. My question is as to which forces, whether it's the military, the Ministry of the Interior, or some other force that is referred to by specialised units. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, but in the spirit of clarification, putting what unit this is, a unit operating within the military structure is extremely important to the defence of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As opposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you can seek further clarification in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel, do you want me to repeat the question or can you respond?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: You can repeat if you want and I can --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: It will be more clarity in the answer I'm going to give to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objections are heard by a witness as well. So if there's anything that spontaneously comes to your mind which would also meet some of the concerns of Mr. Kehoe. I'm not keeping you off from not expressing yourself. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel, if you could say as to whether you had information as to what forces as in -- whether they were -- these were military or Ministry of the Interior or some other forces; and if you have information about exactly what these units were, as Mr. Kehoe just raised, would you please inform us.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Okay, sure. When you read that paragraph 30 in that document, if you go back in that section, that section was titled: Tactics of Croat observed the Croat forces. So what we are talking about here about the units, those were Croat units that were advancing as part of the Operation Storm. Those were the front line units. What I refer and the text refers to there: "Following the success of the units at the front, those were Croats army units at front. Then they were followed by specialise unit. And the term that we used to call those specialised units, in 1995 we call them special force units and they were wearing Balaclavas. Those were the units behind the normal I will say the foot soldiers of the Croat army, but they were more specialised unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document 1731, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel, I think we have the French version now on the screen and we have the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I was informed that we will proceed as follows, that two versions of documents that are originally in French will be uploaded in the system, that is, that finally the English translation and a B/C/S version will be used in court. Not out of disrespect of the French language, of course. But since the originals are in French, I do not mind if the witness is shown the French original version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have -- if the witness wishes to go through the originals, we have hard copies which the witness can be provided with. And for the benefit of everybody else in court we could have the English and the B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar informs me, and I'll check it immediately, that although there should be a B/C/S version uploaded in e-court that there is not actually. And if I look at the source and attachment documents, I see there are only two versions, that is, the French and the B/C/S. Let me just see the original ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I misspoke. As I said before, it's the French original and the English translation. Ms. Mahindaratne, you should take care that a B/C/S version is available as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it causes any practical problems for the Defence teams, they're invited to address me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just to inform you, Mr. President, the B/C/S versions have been served on the Defence, but I will certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- that helps certainly the Defence teams, but might not, for example, help the B/C/S speaking part of the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could find out how we were served that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we go that during the first break or is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you are invited to inform the Defence how they were served.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, is this a report submitted to you by CanBat personnel?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was produced by Charlie Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is a chronological record of events during Operation Storm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who compiled this report or record?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: That was the headquarter of the Charlie Company. Like I said earlier, I -- as part of normal procedure in operations, that each organization, they have duty personnel 24/7 and they log every communications or events in -- happening in their own jurisdiction. And in this instance Charlie Company, they logged what they do during the operation and then they make that, I will say, summary of events.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this document in evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P313 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I call for document number 2563, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the break you may explain also where the B/C/S version of this document is, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, can you identify what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes. That is the sequential events prepared by the headquartered company, and the headquartered company is the company at the battalion level where my ops officer is working.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was this submitted to you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you forward this onwards to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: My recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this document in evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I hear of no objection at this moment. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P314, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P314 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I call up document number 3247, please. It's a set of photographs. I'm sorry, it's not a set of photographs. It's a report. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, you have testified about observing the body of a killed civilian on 9th August in your statements. Is that an accurate report of that incident?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yeah. The only comment I will put on timing at the 620, I think it's quite correct. The 645, it is around that time, it may be a little bit later than that that -- when physically I reach the location of the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, it's not 6, it's 1620 16?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that what you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: 1620 was the first time I saw the individual in the -- at the ends of the Croatian police, but the one after that, 1645, I was informed to return to the location, that timing I cannot say how precise it is. I mean, it's roughly about that, about 45, which is 25 minutes after I saw it; but I thought it was a bit maybe 35, 45 minutes after.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who has compiled this report?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: That was the military police section.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Of the Canadian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this document in evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar, that would be number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P315, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P315 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up document 3254, please. I'm sorry, it's the same document that's coming up. It should be a set of photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter number 03254 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With previous 65 ter number 3247. I'm sorry, it does -- got mixed up. Very well. We'll stick to -- if I could call then for P315. I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have at this moment a series of photographs on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but what has happened is the photographs got attached to the report. So I will stick to P315 and get the witness to confirm the photographs which is at page 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar is nodding in a different direction. Mr. Registrar, could you assist Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the photographs being referenced were in the second 65 ter number given by counsel, which would be 3254.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we have 3254 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, are these the photographs of the body you saw pertaining to which we just looked at a report which is marked and entered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who took these photographs?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: It was either the battalion photograph or the military police themselves, I cannot recall exactly. It's one of the two, because we had photograph at the battalions, that also MPs they have cameras to make pictures of incidents to gather evidence. And those one, I cannot tell whether it was the MP or the battalion photograph, but certainly it was taken by one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you note that near the body there is a canvass bag?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, there is a canvass bag that that old gentleman was carrying. The first time I saw him by the check-point of the Croatian police I suspect it was his own personal belonging in that canvass bag and then -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next page, please, where there's another three sets of photographs I think. And I think there is a third page. Thank you. Mr. President, may these photographs be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Now let's try to get things clear and I'll just check. If you give me one moment, Ms. Mahindaratne. These photographs as they are now uploaded in e-court, that's a document of four pages, the first page is the report, and then three pages with in total nine photograph. Mr. Registrar, is there a chance that we have now the report, if we would admit this document twice in evidence and then one of these reports, that is one of the reports, P315, not with the photographs and what I take it will become P313 -- 16 to be the report plus three pages of photographs. Mr. Registrar, is that the situation we're in at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore I suggest that P315, that the document uploaded will now be replaced by the document that's now uploaded on our screen, that's the report plus three pages in total, nine photographs. And then since there are no objections against the photographs to be attached to the report, we have now the report, a one-page report and three pages of photographs admitted under P315.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up document -- Mr. President, those are the documents tendered in the 92 ter submission. May I proceed with the rest of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be permitted to read a brief summary of the 92 ter submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that you have explained to Mr. Morneau what the purpose of this reading out is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "Colonel Jacques Morneau was a battalion commander of the Canadian battalion referred to as CanBat 1 stationed in the United Nations Sector South within the Krajina from 3rd April to 6th September 1995. He commanded the battalion of 800 personnel, whose principal task was to observe and report on the events within the CanBat area of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Sorry. "Colonel Morneau witnessed systematic looting" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- "of houses and farms by soldiers, members of the military police, and civilians, as well as burning houses in the aftermath of Operation Storm. He further saw a body of an elderly civilian who was seen in the custody of Croatian civilian police immediately prior to his death. Colonel Morneau describes the shelling of the CanBat observation posts and the capture of CanBat personnel attached to the observation posts by the Croatian military based on reports submitted to him by his subordinate personnel." Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, may I just take you to your 2008 statement, and that's the third statement, P310 for the record. And if I could take you to paragraph 8. You referred to the Canadian Battalion consisting of five companies and 800 personnel. Now, of these five companies how many infantry companies were included?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: We had three infantry companies in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How many observation posts did each of the three companies have?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: We had Alpha Company had only two observation posts because the two observation posts were deployed in depth, in fact they were protecting Croats enclaves in the area of the battalion. We had two areas in the battalion that were I will say Croat -- would qualify them as Croat enclaves. It was village of Bruska and the village of Rodaljice --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, we are running a little short of time. If you could say just the number of companies, that would suffice. I'm sorry to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Observation post. Okay. So Alpha Company 2, Bravo Company, they had --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is -- it's not --

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: That's 6 and the other company is 6 also.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that you had 16 observation posts?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: All together, yes, 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now may I call for document number 5162, please. Colonel Morneau, this is a sketch that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Not me personally, but my staff in the battalion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you reproduced this sketch on a map of the Krajina yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, can this sketch be tendered in evidence? He -- the witness has reproduced this on a map of the Krajina to give it context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P316 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And may I call for map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, maps with all kind of signs on it are better to be understood if we get a legend to it so that we know what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will quickly take the witness through the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I take a call for document number -- map number 5174, please. Before that, Mr. President, let me use this sketch map for the explanation so it -- since this is much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, is it correct to say that the positions marked with SC and numbers are the observation posts of the Canadian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, they -- my recollection they were for, in French, Secteur Canadien, SC.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in your reports in English, those same positions are referred to as CS, Canadian sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in the -- towards the middle there are three positions marked with flags, square flags, one under the other. One is connected to a little box with Miranje, the other one to Rastevic, and the third to a box below Kasic. Now, what are those three positions?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: These three positions were camps. We had three camps. The box at Miranje which is labelled C, it says Charlie Company; the one at Rastevic with the number two is for the 2nd Battalion, the Royale 22nd Regiment, which was a battalion number; and the one on the south of Kasic was Bravo Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the numbers indicate the observation post numbering?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: For the SC, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up map 5174, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one more thing. We see the one connected to the box just south of Kasic. We have flee little flags. The top one stands for ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The top one is for the infantry company itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Second one is a platoon, advanced tank platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Third one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Engineer element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now in relation to Rastevic, top one is the same, middle one is different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the admin company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one under is the FR, infantry company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now for Miranje we had as you said already the Charlie --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Infantry company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And there is the reconnaissance platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reconnaissance platoon, thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for map 5174, please. Mr. President, it's a big map. While it comes up, I will ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, now your testimony was that on 6th August when you arrived, eight of your observation posts were captured by the Croatian military. After the six, what happened to the other eight? Were they allowed to operate?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: In fact, they were staying at their location as part of the observation posts themselves, but we had been imposed a restriction of movement by the Croat forces. So we were officially not able to move freely in the area, but we did some movement, we went around the check-points of the Croats army by some small trails to avoid those check-points to be available to either resupply the check-points -- not the check-point but the observation posts or to go to the company -- company locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now we have the map up here and since the locations are too small, Mr. President, for the record, I will read out the markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Starting from the position in the north, the circle, it's Obrovac, the circle at the northern-most point, north towards north-east, it's Obrovac and then clockwise. At the point marked SC 64, Colonel Morneau, it's on your screen, the map, if you have a copy. SC 64, it's Bruska, and the point at SC 65 is Rodaljice. That's R-o-d-a-l-j-i-c-e. The circle next to that is Benkovac. Below that at SC 50 is Pristeg, P-r-i-s-t-e-g. Towards west of that position at CC 07, that's Charlie Company, is Miranje, M-i-r-a-n-j-e. West of that at position SC 45 is Petrim. South-west of that position, the circular is Biograd. North-west from that position at SC 44 is Kakma. North from that position at Bat HQ is Rastovic. Towards north-west of that at SC -- I'm sorry, at SC 53 is Zemunic. North-east of that at SC 40 is Kasic, K-a-s-i-c. And the circular from that point onwards at just above SC 38 is Novi Grad. Now, Colonel Morneau, those are the markings you made yesterday which is a reproduction of your sketch map that you just explained?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this map into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we understand what makes markings in blue and what makes markings in red.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I was -- I completely forgot. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Morneau, when you made these markings you had specific information on the specific grid references with regard to some markings, and those markings where you had the information on grid references, you made with red; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where you did not have the exact grid references and where you had to make approximate markings, where the positions were approximately, you made in blue?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. Any objections? No objections. Mr. Registrar, the map marked by the witness yesterday ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P317 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I call for document number 3990, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now while that's being brought up -- I'm sorry, 3990. I think there is a mistake. The document that's coming up is not --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document that's on the screen is 65 ter number 03990 and it's a document with an original in English consisting of 36 pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's a document titled UNPF CanBat report. I think we have -- we have it here on -- I think we have -- if I may have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The ERN number, if I could assist Mr. Registrar, it's R1041855. We have the document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could please put on the record what you just told me so that we -- this document we see now on our screen is what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, counsel called for 65 ter number 3990, which was the document that was originally brought up on screen; however, the ERN number referenced by counsel, which was R1041855 is in e-court attached as a translation to 65 ter number 3990. However, both documents are English originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which gives you another puzzle for the next break, Ms. Mahindaratne. Do we have on our screen at this moment the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please sort out matters so that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- confusion remains at a minimum level. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Morneau, you testified and you have referred to in your first statement that the CanBat reported or compiled a report on the human rights violations which included reports on pillaging and burning recorded by your battalion in August 1995. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is this a document that's -- that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this document in evidence. Before that, Mr. President, this document has several annexes which contain sensitive information with regard to victims, so may it be tendered under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Mahindaratne, you say it has several annexes. I see that it's a five-page document. I do not see any annexes at this moment to this document, unless you are referring to information we find on the pages following --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, in fact I think the correct -- although it's only the first five pages that have been uploaded to the e-court, but this is a very big document with several annexes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, it's fine to know that your version of this document contains a lot of information which is not part of what, of course, this Chamber is admitting. So I see that on the second page of this document we get specific cases of human rights violations; on the third it starts with general violations and then pillaging, burning of private property and then a few other categories there; on the fourth page we find a new heading before paragraph 17, mistreatment of UN soldiers; and on the last page we only have paragraph 18. If you are seeking protection on the basis of what we find in annexes which are not attached to this document, then we have a rather empty request, isn't it? It doesn't -- but I have not scanned the document on any information about victims. Could you perhaps after the break inform the Chamber whether for the five documents you are tendering into evidence now, whether the protection by admitting it under seal is needed or not needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. For these five pages it's not necessary. I was -- I intended to tender the entire document so that the document would be complete. However the information I wished to place before the Trial Chamber is in the main document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is in the main document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So the necessity for it to be tendered under seal at this stage is not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections. Mr. Registrar, what would be the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the five pages mentioned by counsel that are ERN number R1041855 become Exhibit P318.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I realize I'm running out of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes, the ERN number just mentioned by Mr. Registrar is the first ERN number of these -- of this five-page document and is admitted into evidence as Exhibit P318. Ms. Mahindaratne, here of course it is presented as a document attached to another document, apparently being its translation, but that cannot be true because both these documents are in English. So therefore, a B/C/S version of this document is still required.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, during the break I will find out as to what has happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge. Was it the map itself that became 317, Mr. Monkhouse?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was this five-page report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Monkhouse said that was 318.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 318. Then I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I find on page 31, line 6, that the five-page document is P318 and that is the document that we are looking at at this moment. But I think I admitted -- I'm looking at page 31, line 11, that this five-page document was admitted under P318. So from what I see at this moment on my screen, there seems to be no inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I'm aware I'm running out of time, but I have a few more areas to call if I may seek the Court's indulgence to provide me with just ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that you announced one and a half hours earlier and that you said that you most likely would do with less. In view of what the Defence indicated, we should have sufficient time this morning. You will not run to any difficulties if Ms. Mahindaratne will take another 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, that will be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, when you were interviewed in 2006 you handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor a videotape which contained footage of deployment of the Canadian Battalion as well as some scenes of destruction after Operation Storm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that footage recorded by one of your subordinate personnel?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it done pursuant to your instructions?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I mean throughout the -- our deployment we had also as part of the battalion a public information officer, and I had given him a task at the beginning of the deployment to collect footage of the front activities of the battalion throughout its deployment with the intent that at the end of the deployment we'll put together those footage and make, as I said, as a kind of a memory for the soldiers, and I made reproduction of those cassettes to each of the soldiers, so each of the soldiers of the battalion receive a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, what was the area you asked your personnel to film in terms of the destruction? Was it your area of responsibility or Sector South? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, mainly in the area of the CanBat 1, but it may appear that there was some footage that they were taking between our battalion and Knin, which then passed outside our area of responsibility into the Canadian Battalion area of responsibility towards the city of Knin. But I will say that the ballpark was in the CanBat 1 AOR and maybe some footage, like I said, on the roads towards Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to play the tape. We'll play only 50 seconds of it, but there's a 4 minute and 22 seconds of footage I move to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, any text spoken on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. There is just three words at the beginning which is very clear, but there is no text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The 65 ter number is 3756, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if she's only playing 50 seconds, if I can just get -- on the break look through the rest of what's being tendered that's not being played and just reserve at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We could stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Morneau, do you recognise that footage as being the footage recorded by your CanBat personnel?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And are you able to say generally, not -- you don't have to be very specific if you don't have recollection what this area is?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly where it was in the area, but it was part of the Sector South for sure and more likely in the -- in my battalion area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender that footage into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear from the Defence so we just now mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P319, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, may I take you to your statement, the first statement, that is -- I beg your pardon, the third statement, 2008, to paragraph 6. In paragraph 6 you refer to communicating with the Croatian liaison officer regarding the release of your captured personnel, and you also say even in relation to other matters. Whom do you mean by Croatian liaison officer? And I'm not asking for a name. Is it HV liaison officer or liaison officer for the government? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: That was the CALO in Zadar and CALO standed for Croatian army liaison officer in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. And moving you to your first statement if you go to your 1996 statement and there the paragraphs are not numbered. If you go to page 3, from the top it's paragraph 6 if you count from the top of the page. You refer to your freedom of movement of the CanBat being denied by Croats. Now, what was the manner in your free -- in which your freedom of movement was restricted? How was it done? Could you answer briefly?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, following or during and following the Operation Storm the Croats army and then -- and then after that, the Croats military police and then eventually the Croat civilian police, they established roadblocks all over the area. I mean, they were -- to enter the zone of the -- what we used to call the Krajina, the zone of separation between the Croats armed forces and the Serbian armed forces, there were entry points to the area of responsibility and there were check-points in those areas plus throughout the area there were additional check-points to control any movement. So if we were to attempt to move ourselves, so we were stopped at those check-points and they were refusing the right of passage to the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you say following the operation, when did you see these check-points? Is it immediately following the operation or can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, they were established right after the first wave of the leading troops. As soon as the leading troops would pass an area then there were check-point established initially by the Croat army, military police, and then eventually replaced by Croats civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could I ask for a clarification as far as the comma is concerned. I invite you, Mr. Morneau, to look at the screen. I take it that you have text in front of you as well, 36, line 12 puts a comma after Croat army, which makes it initially by the Croat army, military police, and then eventually replaced by Croats civilian police. Another way of reading it without the comma would be: Initially by the Croat army military police and then eventually replaced by Croats civilian police. Are you talking about three stages, the first one Croat army, second one military police, and then Croatian civilian police; or were you talking about two stages, the first one Croat army military police and then eventually replaced by Croats civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning during the period of the offensive, the Croat army itself was busy with the -- fighting the fight, I will say; and following that it was the military police that was establishing the check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So no check-points established by military not being military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say no. It may have happened in some circumstances somewhere that the military itself established check-points, but I will say as a measure of process. I mean they were -- the troops were fighting the fight and the military police were establishing check-points but it may have happened in some areas that there were no military police, that then the military itself will establish check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, can I take you to page 4 of your -- of the same statement, 1996. And to -- from the top of the page, paragraph 2, you go on to say that: "On many occasions I saw at the beginning Croats in military uniforms and then civilians looting houses. On some occasions I witnessed people coming out from houses with looted articles. When I passed the houses again on my return I saw the same houses burning." Now, my question to you is: With regard to those occasions, and I appreciate you can't speak with regard to each and every occasion, but those occasions when you pass houses where you saw people coming out with looted goods and then when you return you saw those same houses on fire, who were those people you saw coming out of the houses with the looted goods? And I'm referring to those houses which were on fire later on. Were they military or civilian or both?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Initially were military, and then eventually there were a mix of military and civilian. And as the time went by, there were more and more civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And during the first week after the operation, who had control of your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: The Croat army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could take you back, Colonel Morneau, and these are my couple of last questions, to page 2 from the top, paragraph 4. I'm sorry, I think I got the wrong page. I think it's page 4, paragraph 2. That same paragraph we were on at -- earlier on. You go on to say: "My opinion about what happened during the month of August 1995 is that the higher Croatian authorities closed their eyes to the fact that there was systematic looting and burning of houses in all of my area of responsibility." Now, my question to you, Colonel, is: What do you mean by systematic looting and destruction? Can you clarify that a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I will say that in a normal situation you may have a riot in a city that you have looting that happens at the occasion of that riot. In this instance it was not one incident. It was day after day and after day for thee to four weeks and it was very deliberate in a sense that it was not -- there were a selection of the houses. I mean, some houses were not touched and some houses were burned. So there were a pattern, a scheme, to go and loot and then burn those houses. And at the beginning like I said it, it was only with the soldiers but quickly there were civilians that were with the soldiers and the -- I don't know, probably the -- probably they were living in the area in the past so they knew exactly who the house belonged to and who used to live in those houses. So it was a process, I will say, that -- because even some houses that have seen some houses that have been burning two or three different times. I mean there's quite resilient houses and they are built in the cement blocks and it's not like North America, when it burns, it burns down to the ground. But there were some places it was surprising to see that the same house would be put on fire again. So when I say systematic, I mean because it was a repetition of it. It was not one incident. It was a constant process that was taking place for three to four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Taking you to your last statement, Colonel Morneau, that is 2008 statement, paragraph 9. And actually, paragraph 9 going on to page 3 so I'm looking at the top of the paragraph. You refer to freedom of movement -- restrictions on freedom of movement and you say: "The Croatians informed us that the restriction was while they cleared the area of pockets of Serbian resistance but our observations indicated that the restriction was also used to conduct looting and destruction." Now, can you tell the Court as to what were those observations that led you to come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, when they were blocking off some specific area with check-points we could not enter to observe what was happening in that area. I will take the example of the city of Benkovac whereby there were check-points all around the access road to go there. And then we could not see what was happening inside, but what we could see was a lot of vehicles coming out of that area with looted furniture or farm equipment or cattles, whatever they were looting, they were coming out of the same area that we could not get in. So I don't know the reason, was it just to make sure that we were not going to witness what they were doing and then they were looting and then they -- to do it more I will say anonymously. That was our presumption, that because of the restriction of freedom of movement to those specific area and seeing all those equipment coming out of it at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My last question to you, Colonel Morneau, and that is based on your first statement. Let me take you to your 1996 statement again. I'm sorry for going to and fro. If I could take you to page 4 of the 1996 statement, and from the top paragraph 4, referring to the criminal activity you say: "On some occasions I sent my subordinates to ask the HV liaison office in Zadar the reason for the burning and looting and why they allowed it. I can recall that the Croats reply was that they couldn't control it." Now, is that many -- was that statement consistent with what you observed the situation to be?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Not at all. I mean -- I mean, we reported day after day to the CALO, the Croatian army liaison officer in Zadar what was happening in the area of responsibility, and we told them that, hey, they should take a control or grip on their soldiers and their military police and their civilian police. But an action like that that happened over three or four weeks, I mean with all of the chain of command that was in place, with all of the check-points that was in place, it would have been very hazy if there were an order passed down the chain of command to say we don't want any looting happening and there were so many people all over the place that it would have been impossible to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I said it was my last question but one follow-up question, Colonel Morneau. The presence of the units on the ground as you saw it, were they organized units or were they soldiers just coming into the area in a random fashion?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I think they were both. Some were organized units. I will say that the first wave of the Croat army was more the regular force, better trained, better equipped, and then there were some conscript forces that were, I will say, holding the ground. They were left behind in the AOR to control the area with military police and then eventually more and more civilian police. So they were specific units and Croatian army units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Perhaps I would like to seek further clarification of your last answer. Do I understand you well that there first was a wave of, let's say, combat units. Did they participate in or did they -- were they involved in these looting activities as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say if they were all involved. For sure, that the first wave they were passing through and they were fighting the fight, so there were not time to do looting, but the one that they were staying in place -- I mean, my understanding was that the best troops were moving towards Knin and that area to the capital. And then following that, some have been redeployed and some have been -- also there were some units from the -- what I call the conscript units that were less best equipped, that they were also in the area but they were still formed units from the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so these were the troops that were left behind and were not at the front line, and you said they operated still as units, not as individuals but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- units --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you give me a clue as to when you talk about units, is it about -- I take it first of all a plurality of persons, more persons, not just one? How many --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, military unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, military units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a sense -- as an example, they establish a headquarter in Benkovac, so it's nothing at all they would establish a headquarter, it is a formed unit and they were a formed unit in Benkovac that there was established there. So they were occupying -- they were the occupying force, I will say, of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what others will call liberating force, but I leave that to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Occupy the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as neutral. Yes, occupy the ground. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But also over time, after X number of days, after one week, there were the front troops, some of them came back to the rear also. So when the wave was passed some of that first wave came back in the area. I won't say all of them. Some were redeployed to Split and other places. But we saw some of the troops that were initially passed through, some of the individuals came back. In fact, I remember having a conversation that one of the officers I believe that after a week he came back and he was kind of surprised to see himself that much destruction that had been happening in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So these forces were -- this was an organized presence. Now, was it also organized looting? Would they go one by one or would they go in small groups or would they go in units? Was there any system in, for example, go in a group house by house or -- I'm trying to understand exactly to what extent this was just individual misbehaviour or whether this was misbehaviour collective for the units the individuals were in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say that it was organized and directed, but I will say that it was easily preventable because of the deployment of all those units on the ground, if there had been an order to say there is no looting in our area then there would not have been any looting. Having said that, I mean, if you had a sealed area like we had some -- like in Benkovac like the example I gave earlier, I mean, there are check-points there that we cannot enter so we cannot witness what was happening. So was it organized from the chain of command or was it the fact that we didn't want to look -- for us to look at that. That's lead me to believe that there was some level of organization there that they didn't want us to witness what was happening in those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You deduce the level of organization more from the measures apparently taken to keep you out of the area than from a direct observation on whether any instructions were given or how they actually operated, that is, in what kind of groups or whether or not under any orders, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you did not observe -- I have some difficulties in -- I said that the level of organization that you deduced that rather from the measures apparently taken to keep you out than from direct observation. Then you said the latter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I didn't see an officer directing people, go and empty that house. I have not seen those actions. What we saw is people coming out of building so for the places would seem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were those just individuals, was it one person going in, coming out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Small groups of individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Small groups, and then you're talking about, what is a small group for you? Three or four, eight to nine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be two, three guys to six, seven, eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could I ask just one question, just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, Ms. Mahindaratne, but I'm really looking at the clock now because you have got your last question and then another question and now very last question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel Morneau, during the first week after the operation you referred to your statements observing what you call systematic looting and destruction. During the first week did you observe that, first week after the operation --

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is asked and answered now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then have a break. The question has -- the question has been answered by a yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're the first one to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Morneau, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record I drew a potential correction to the attention of Mr. Monkhouse on the break on page 43, line 16 where I think it's listed as construction and I believe the witness said destruction. I think it's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Usually comments on the transcript are best to be delivered to the transcribers unit because they have to take care of it and they'll verify whether your version is any better than theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, of course, it's appreciated, Mr. Kehoe. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to talk about a few subjects that were discussed on your direct examination and then some other topics that you discuss in your statements. I would like to talk first about the murders that you talked about and we saw a series of photographs that came into evidence of an old man, a dead body that you had seen in the field. And I believe that you stated in your testimony that he had been in the custody of the civilian police prior to that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the other incident that came to our attention was a matter that was brought up in three -- P318, if we could take 318 up on the screen. Colonel, this is also a matter that I believe you discussed in your statement at various occasions, but I believe cryptically it's probably better just to go at this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please, of the document, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can look at paragraph 7, Colonel, it has to do with a Mr. Stegnajic coming to the camp first on the 17th and then later on the 21st of August, and this is listed under specific cases of human rights violations and it notes that "her body was examined and no external signs of force being used were found." If I can turn your attention to P233, and it is a -- P233, Colonel, is a UNCIVPOL incident report. If we could look at that, it notes CIVPOL, and this is the same Mr. Stegnajic, and it notes the preliminary incident after him coming to the CanBat 1 gate he related that on the 21st of August, this is four lines down, two men dressed in civilian clothes with long hair and carrying AK-47s came to his house. Were you informed of that, Colonel?
