utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: As part of the -- I was informed when the individual -- my recollection is one -- on the 21st when he came and then he asked for assistance and then I sent the MP with them to investigate what was happening with his wife. My recollection at that time was that, yes, he mentioned that to the -- to my staff and then this is when I decided to dispatch the MP there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So he mentioned that -- he mentioned that two men in civilian clothes had come with long hair; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I try to remember now. Because I didn't speak to him personally. I mean, what was -- it was my staff. He came to the gate and spoke with people at the gate and my recollection was that there were some people that came to his house and were threatening -- threatening his wife and his -- himself to -- if they were not leaving that there will be consequences to his wife and himself. But I cannot say who it was as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just waiting for the translation to catch up, Colonel. If we can go back down about halfway down the page. When your MPs took him back to the scene did they note, as reflected in this report, that the woman was dead in the water. Tied to the wall of the well was her cane, and immediately to the front of the well was her apron neatly folded and her shoes placed on top. Did they tell you that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I saw that as part of that report. Not those details -- I was not told that -- what I was told after that fact was that they discovered a lady in the well, but I had not been provided verbally the details, so it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were provided these by your MPs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did they tell you or comment to you that they believed it was a suicide by this man's wife?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: No. I mean, they didn't mention to me that it was a suicide. But personally I did some linkage because it was not the first day. It started the 17th and then when the gentleman came back it was the 21st. And following that he had been threatened, and then the -- he had to leave, he had to escape himself and asked for help and we went back with him. I mean, if you are threatened -- I don't know, I don't know what happened there, but you can make different deductions from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. If I could just change subjects, sir, and go back to your statement, 309, your 1996 statement. And I'm referring to the comments that you talked about on cross about -- that's a third full paragraph down, they went on some occasions.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 4. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph, I believe it's the first -- excluding the carryover paragraph, the third full paragraph: "On some occasions ..." This is the one you said you sent your subordinates to --

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the latter part it says: "I can recall that the Croat reply was that they couldn't control it." Now, Colonel, were you aware of steps that were being taken by the Croatian authorities to attempt to control this looting and burning, both on the military side and on the civilian side, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: No, I mean I was not aware and I have not seen any evidence on the ground that there were any attempt to control it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if orders were given and some of this still happened with units, it would bring into question the effective control over those units, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But suffice it to say at this point without going into it at some length, you were unaware of any efforts being made by civilian authorities and military authorities to curtail this activity?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Not at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted during the course of your testimony this morning that some of this looting was taking place by civilians and soldiers together. Now, if we can turn to your 2008 statement for some clarity on this score, that is P310.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The bottom paragraph. You note on page -- I guess that's paragraph 9 you note that: "I describe the looting that I witnessed by the military and civilians. Most of the vehicles I saw were civilian vehicles with a mixture of military and civilian drivers." Is that accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on your long distinguished career, sir, I mean military and civilians don't -- the military don't normally operate in conjunction with civilians when they're conducted military operations, do they?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Normally no. If I may add some comment here. During that phase after the wave of the offensive, there were more and more civilian coming in the area and we saw civilian with military, were they working together, were they talking, but we saw many instances that there were civilian accompanied by military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us just take that. There were civilians then coming back into the area where they had formerly lived. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: In a manner of saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was what you deducted by the civilians coming back in?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yeah, there may have been others not living there, living close by, like Zadar or Split, they were curious and -- or might be tempted by coming and looting and certainly some were ex-inhabitant of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, when you observed this did you conclude that these people that were conducting these looting and burning activities were engaged in a degree of revenge in that they were trying to take back things that had been taken from them some years prior to that by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, I cannot ascertain if it was revenge. We get -- the only thing I can say is the facts that they were doing those actions. What motives, it's up to them to describe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I have some difficulties with understanding your question in full detail. You're using the word revenge, which as far as I understand, is doing a similar thing to what has been done to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at the same time you are talking about trying to take back things that had been taken from them some years prior to that by the Serbs. Now, if you look at it at an abstract level, that is you have taken -- well, let's say property or land from the Croatians, now we take back land, then it's a kind of restitution of an earlier situation. If we are talking on a mini level, then it would be, you've taken my fridge, now I take my fridge back. These are different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or the functional equivalent of your fridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. But then revenge, taking back what was taken from you at least leaves open some of these questions. Therefore, I have some difficulties in how I would have to interpret that question before I could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I understand, Judge, and I think the witness said that he couldn't -- he couldn't assess the motivations of those individuals at the time. So I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I add a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had 23 -- up to 23 refugee that came to our camp, and as part of these refugees coming to our camp we did interview them as they were coming, as to what happened. And we asked them to make statements. And I believe that those statements were -- are the annexes that were referred to this morning about the human rights violations. From what I -- from what we gathered from a number of those different individuals that were coming to our camp, I mean they did -- some of them did recognise some of the civilians, probably they were from the same area, but then they were threatened by those same civilians who were accompanied by military soldiers to leave the area because there were no business for them anymore. So is it that attitude or behaviour, is it a revenge because they were expelled from their area? I mean, that could qualify as a revenge if they -- now they were threatening them -- the same civilians to leave the area or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes thank you for that clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that score, Colonel, about these interviews coming back, was it from these interviews of refugees coming to your camp that you received this information about units wearing these Balaclavas, these masks?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: No, that was from the people of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, on that score from your battalion, did the battalions or the people in your battalion, did they designate whether or not this unit wearing this Balaclava was part of a particular formation?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Not a specific formation, but the way they described them, it was -- they were a form -- unit a former group of people who were doing that special duty and they were calling them special force. Were they special force or not, I cannot say, but they were specialised troops doing that specific task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know if they were civil or military?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to P312, the first page of this -- of P312. If I can just -- now, those are the brigades that your report notes were deployed in your sector. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to paragraph 30 two pages up. Is that, in fact, two pages up? It was actually the page that was discussed by counsel this morning, 707854. I can ask the question, Colonel, without that. In the area of the report that discusses these units, this -- with wearing these Balaclavas, none of those four units that you described in the report is listed in that paragraph. Is there any -- I mean, did they not see any military designations on these units or they simply just not identified where they were from?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: They didn't identify which unit they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, turning back to our subject of the actual looting, and if we could go to P316 -- and before we go to -- as we're bringing that up I'll continue to ask some preliminary questions on this score. In your commentary on 308, quickly go back to P308, and on 308 in the -- page 4 of the first full paragraph you note in the last sentence, you're talking about the systematic looting and burning: "It would have been very easy to prevent all these things from happening." Now, Colonel, to prevent these things from happening you obviously need check-points; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe you noted in response to a question by Judge Orie that at least initially the check-points were military police and then civilian police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Initially, yes, but it depends where in the area. I mean, there were a mix of check-points, military check-points and civilian check-points at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just look at a check-point, Colonel. At an individual check-point if you were to put a check-point at that location, how many individuals would you need to man that check-point on a 24-hour basis, seven days a week?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: It would depend how you want to drive your soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's say eight-hour shifts.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Normally six soldiers will do a good job at that check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we had six soldiers in -- what would you say, six soldiers in eight-hour shifts, right? So that's how many soldiers, are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Not necessarily an eight-hour shift. You can have six soldiers at a check-point, that they will be able to man it 24/7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. But obviously you don't have soldiers there on a 24-hour basis and they need sleep and rest and to be fed, and as a commander if you were setting up a check-point at a location, how many soldiers would you deploy, given all the humanitarian -- humanitarian concerns involved, I mean, eating, sleeping, et cetera, how many would you put at a check-point?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Between six and ten. To give an example, all the observation point that we had deployed, there were sections or level and there were between six, seven soldiers at a time because we had a vacation plan that they are always 25 per cent away and normally the section was nine people. So you had seven soldiers at an observation point and they were manning the observation point 24/7. So you can apply the same rationale to a check-point and then with a section of six to ten, six, seven on the location and some others that are going on leave or rest and then you can man a check-point with a section easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just -- maybe you can help me clarify some of the numbers. When you have a unit of men or soldiers or policemen at a check-point, taking into consideration people on leave, taking into consideration rest, taking into consideration being at a check-point out in the elements, when you bring that whole total together, how many would you as a colonel deploy at that check-point to say, Now, you soldiers have to control that check-point? What's the total number?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: A section of ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ten. Now, in addition to the ten at the check-point, would you have other soldiers or police in the area combing the area to make sure that the check-point wasn't threatened in some other fashion off the road?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I will not say threatened, but if you want to have a positive control in an area you establish that check-points and then you establish patrols and then you send patrols in between check-points and to cover the areas that the check-point does not necessarily cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the patrols would be a number of soldiers in addition to the ten soldiers that you have at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, but it can be a mix of the two. I mean, you can have your own check-point depending on the situation. If it is a quiet check-point, then they can go on their own, send two men patrolling the area and come back to the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If it's an active check-point, then obviously you would --

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: They need more manpower to handle the traffic and what's happening at that check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in the check-point you also when you're looking as to whether or not things are quiet or happening in your area, would you take into consideration that there were 40.000 displaced Croats that wanted to come back into the Krajina? Would that part of the -- something you would take into consideration in determining how many people to deploy at a check-point along with the patrols?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: That's dependent of intent of the military commander. What kind of situation he has analysed he will face. So does the check-point -- is to control the movement within the OR for whatever reason, and then you assess, okay you have potential Serb straddlers, you have the UN element that are in the area, and you have also like you just said potential returnees that want to go back to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, they -- people started to return to this area -- but let me go back to this report, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm trying to reference the actual P numbers. It's P314, paragraph 52. I'm sorry, with all due respect, my French is not what it should be. French was up on the screen, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, if we look at paragraph 15 of the item on the 6th of August it talks about -- paragraph 52, I apologise, on the screen, Colonel, it talks about some burning and looting going on, but it also says: "In addition Croats were reoccupying the houses along the eastern part of the security zone." Do you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, they were coming back as early as a day after the end of Operation Storm. Were they coming back in large numbers that early, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Not in big groups. They would come more individually, but I didn't see a mass of civilian coming at once. They were -- I think on one day you see a house is empty and then the next day you come and you have civilian in the house. That's part of the I will say that support that statement that was re-occupying those houses. I mean we knew from the past there were no people in those houses and then over time they were coming back in those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, when did you return to Sector South? I know that you weren't there during Operation Storm. When did you come back?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: The 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The 6th, that day?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going again with this idea that there were returnees and you noted for us that you would have ten at the check-point, if you had the need for patrolling, how many additional soldiers might you need above the ten?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: It depends -- it depends the area that you have to cover, the wider and bigger the area, the more patrol you will need to have proper control of the area, but it depends on the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand it's a question that is fact-oriented with the area, but if we had ten, if you were a commander in a check-point that was of medium activity, how many additional soldiers might you need?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Patrols are not related to a check-point. They are related to a surface, an area to cover. I mean the bigger the area, the more patrol you will need if you want to have a proper control of the area. So it's really -- if you have one square kilometre versus 100 square kilometres, your answer will be different so that give me an area or a size of an area, and we can discuss about the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about Sector South as a whole, if you wanted patrols, how many would you need?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Sector South as a whole, I mean lots of patrols, I mean it would be many, many patrols because you had the Czech battalion AOR, the Jordanian battalion, the Canadian and the Kenyan. To cover all of that you need lots of patrol to have a complete control. But patrolling is one way of controlling. If -- you can achieve as much a good control with check-points, so if you have a good check-point system in place, which they had in the area, I mean you have a positive control. I mean, you may have some people that will bypass, but it will be minor as opposed to large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you say that you would need just in Sector South something in the area of four battalions to do that kind of patrolling?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I will say that with four battalions you will have a very good patrol system because Sector South we had four battalions, and in fact you don't need that many just to patrol. If you want to occupy the ground you will need that many. Just to give you an example, we had four battalions in Sector South, but we were occupying mainly the zone of separation. So most of our troops were tied up in the zone of separation on the static observation post, and like in my own AOR we had two companies tied up in the zone of separation because they had to -- that was the most sensible area. But they had the third company, the reserve company, had a full company that was in charge of patrolling all the rest of the AOR. So with a full company they were covering the complete AOR. So you don't need four battalions just to patrol. If you want to have a control of the area with the check-point and patrol, then you may end up with four battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, we're now in a long series of questions about what you would need to have an effective system of check-points and control, isn't it? However, but just the testimony of this witness is that the check-points let just the looted material go. That's at least -- so it seems that we are -- I, for example, draw your attention to page 4 of the witness's first statement: "I saw vehicles with looted articles go through the check-points all over my AOR. Sometimes I saw the police stop the driver and ask questions and then let it go." So it seems that there are two different discussions, the one is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I disagree, Judge, because I'm trying to develop the rest of the point on what's involved and what's necessary to put in that area, and I'm going into another subarea, moving away from the actual numbers and moving into the other qualifications of the people at those check-points. So we are talking about a series of numbers, putting aside soldiers who were actually in combat but also those who were actually manning check-points and doing patrols and what's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then -- I was just a bit afraid that we are dealing with two rather distinct issues, but if you bring them together I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- carefully listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I beg for a little indulgence as I go through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You know a bit of my impatience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. But I wish things were as easy as writing on a piece of paper and handing it in, but there is a distinct disadvantage when statements come across the bar with conclusions that we have to confront the witness not only pursuant to the rules but the requirements of the Chamber, and that's what I'm attempting to do with the colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition, Colonel, we are talking about the elements involved as a commander. The people that you put out at check-points and on patrol have to have training in order to do the job properly, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And has -- has it been your experience that they have to have the available equipment, they have to have the correct equipment in order to do the proper job, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Check-point, you don't need much equipment. I mean, you need a physical presence and to be able to stop traffic and verify the identity of the people passing through. So that's the purpose of a check-point. So you don't need any equipment to do that. I mean, you have people standing on the street, they do a check-point. If you want to have more protection, you have vehicles, you can make some other improvisation to stop vehicles if they were to try to force the check-point, but it's the level of threat or injury that you anticipate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, at minimum, Colonel, you would agree that they would need hopefully uniforms, some type of weapons, and some type of transportation, that would be a minimum requirement?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: They will need weapons, that's for sure, vehicles to go to the check-point, but then the check-point itself, you may leave the people there and they man the check-point without vehicles. I mean, normally, preferably, you will have but it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In addition to that, when you go into an area to either man a check-point or do the reconnaissance patrolling, you need a knowledge of the area also, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: You don't need any knowledge for check-points. If you want to patrol, then you need to have at least a map so you know where you want to -- where you are and where you are going, especially if you are given instruction or orders to patrol a specific area. Then normally you will need a -- either a map or a very good knowledge of the area, one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, did you know how many men the HV military police had in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, even with check-points, if we turn our attention to your first statement at P308 on page 3, and the second-last paragraph from the bottom, talking about check-points. Do you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you note that on the second sentence: "During my time -- during this time," we're talking about around August 11th, "I managed to take the small roads in the AOR around the Croat check-points to visit my troops and were able to resupply the company camps." If we go to your 2003 statement, if I could just get the P number on that score, that is P309, paragraph 12. The first half of that sentence you said: "I decided to avoid the civilian check-point." So, Colonel, you and the other CanBat soldiers were getting around these check-points relatively easily, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yeah, but we had military vehicles and we can go off road with military vehicle more easily than a normal commercial pattern vehicle or a car because a car off road doesn't work like a jeep or an APC, armoured personnel carrier. And then I will say what we've seen in the area, most of the people looting were using the main roads, they were not using small roads because they could not travel over those small roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one just brief moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, let me take a look at P317.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's going to go up on the screen, Colonel. Now, Colonel, this is the map that you talked about your observation posts upon, but there are numerous roads in and around those observation points in your sector, both main roads and side roads, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I will say there were a few roads and many trails.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us go to a map that maybe we can see some of this a little bit better, and that would be 1D270036. Colonel, these are a series of roads in the south-east corner of Sector South, basically your AOR, area of responsibility. And it sets forth here main roads and side roads through various villages, as you can see. And in your statement of P308 on page 4 you note that it would have been very easy to prevent looting and burning. Based on this map and these roads, Colonel, how many check-points would have been needed in your area to stop the looting and the burning?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I will not say the numbers. I mean, you would have to do an assessment for that, but were on the ground at the time we were there because there were check-points all over the places and especially around the villages and the main access roads, I mean those locations I didn't add up how many Croat armies check-point there were all together, but there were a lot of them, all over the place there were check-points. So I cannot give you a number here, but the only comment I will say that the amount that was there deployed on the ground was sufficient to have a positive control of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Using a, with the assistance of the usher, Colonel, just with the assistance of the usher could you use a pen and mark on this map the potential check-points that you believe would have been needed to prevent this activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to confess, I can't quite see what area we are looking at here. The top of the map says UNCRO Sector South - South-east corner, if we could focus --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the south-east corner as opposed to just taking an area in the north which is also just north of Srb which is also part of Sector South that obviously has no pertinence to the Colonel's responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can blow that up more if you want, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: That will be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise if it's a little difficult. Just orient yourself, Colonel. You can see Zadar, the city of Zadar on the left-hand side and then Benkovac. Is that good? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Okay. As you can see, the size of the -- the scale that we have now, we can start to make sense of what we see there. But to control I will say the traffic, you look at the main roads going in the area. If you are to put a check-point there and then a check-point coming to the -- because what I -- what is in blue is a zone of separation that you have put there on your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: So if you put the main street coming in in the AOR itself, I mean from the north, and then it's right there, so those are the main ones. And I will concentrate, I will say and they put there -- they put this one -- in fact, if you were forming -- to keep it simple, we'll do it closer to the zone of separation to avoid if you want to have any people coming into the area or -- because the zone of separation was also mined and people were concerned to go to the zone of separation in a minefield. So they will tendency to keep on the street. So if you want to control the area itself so you establish your entry points, potential entry points that you see on the map in the zone of separation, that will be easier and you need less check-point to have a control going in and out. But in addition of it, if you want to control inside the area you may add some others depending on the area that you want to control. I mention the city of Benkovac, that there were check-points all around the city of Benkovac on the main artery to control the access. So that's an example of how you establish control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, you've placed no Xs on any of these smaller roads coming into Sector South between those check-points, did you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: It depends of the quality of the dirt road. I mean, some are very rough dirt road that you cannot go with trucks or civilian cars. You need an armoured personnel carrier or a jeep to go on those trails. So from the map here I cannot say which one is good enough for traffic, I will say normal traffic, versus military vehicle traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted for us that some of them were very difficult roads, but from your observations you noticed that people were moving quite regularly on these side roads with vehicles, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness never testified to that effect. The testimony was that the witness and his -- the CanBat took routes avoiding the check-points, not people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I note in his testimony at line 15: "Some were very rough dirt roads that you cannot go with trucks or civilian cars."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my question is: There were other roads, other dirt roads that you observed people, civilians, et cetera, travelling on right easily, very easily, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: What I observed is -- you see the main arteries, those were the paved roads. Those were the ones that you saw the most of the -- I will say -- I will not say convoy, but many, many vehicles with looting effect. But the people were leaving throughout the area, so they were going to a specific house and then taking whatever in the house and then going to the closest distance to the main road and then go out of the Krajina, out of the -- towards the -- towards Croatia per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Morneau, could I ask you one question. The area you just covered by these markings what you would consider the number of check-points you would need to exercise control over this looting, how many check-points actually were there? So apart from where you would put them, but could you give us an approximate number of the area you just now filled in with your projected check-points? How many were there approximately in total?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a good question. In that specific area of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- well, let's say the area you considered when marking your check-points on this map, that same area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- are you referring to the check-point that the Croats had in place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that actually you described in your statement and your testimony, that there were check-points.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So on this whole area how many check-points actually were in place, so apart from how many you would need and where you would put them, but in total.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will say that there were maybe between 30 and 50 check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber when you -- I mean, the witness marked ten check-points he said he would need and then you say but you didn't mark any. But of course the -- let's not lose ourselves in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There are more check-points if we move up the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just move this up a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kehoe, when you invited the witness to mark where he would put his check-points, the Chamber exchanged -- the Judges exchanged as their own position that this was not a very helpful exercise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can we move this page up a bit and if we can rotate down to the Drnis area -- Your Honour, I understand if we could move this into evidence and move it down the page because I understand that I can't move this after markings are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, zooming in and out and moving I think is not possible once it -- however, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I first please deal with the very technical matter of this map. Ms. Mahindaratne, any objection against this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D286.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. D286 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The marking I put on the map, the marking is an illustration where I will put is not a complete analysis where I put them all. I mean -- I mean, that's just to illustrate what type of locations, but if you want to do an exhaustive study about the area and then you want to control the area and then you have to add up a lot more of those check-points there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can bring this exhibit back up without the markings on it. And we can just scroll up a bit to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, looking at this particular area going through, going down from Benkovac you would put yet more check-points on this border area as well, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just -- if you can, just mark those areas as well.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: But now I am outside my battalion AOR there, that's the Kenyan Battalion AOR there on the east. But that's for the -- I will say the X I just put there again is for the entry point in the AOR. Maybe could add another here if the trail is -- depending on the quality of that trail. You have to access it from the ground, what is the access, is it is a trail that was use, that was usable or not, then if it is potential access, you put a check-point. If there is no traffic or no potential for traffic, you don't put a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So potentially you're talking about quite a few check-points depending on whether or not these are passable roads; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now -- Your Honour, I'll move this into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D287, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D287 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going back to a question, to follow up a question that Judge Orie asked you about and I think you responded about people with property coming through the check-points.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it was observed that that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't know whether or not those people were getting back their property or stealing someone's property, do you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, getting back their property is impossible for me to assess. I mean, they were bringing a lot of material, farm equipment, furniture and cattles and everything that was coming from the area. Who it belongs, I mean for the past number of years it was Serbs that were living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you mentioned something this morning about soldiers coming back. The front line soldiers who had passed through that were very upset about the destruction that they saw --

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mentioned one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: One officer that I spoke, that he came back the following week and he was surprised to see how much destruction there had been because the first wave didn't have time to burn houses and destroy, but it was the following troops and the following people behind the first wave that did that destruction. But like I said, the second week after the -- there was some redeployment of the troops, they didn't stay on the border with Bosnia. Some were redeployed to Split, some were redeployed in the area to take positions. I don't know what plan they had, but we saw some coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And some of these -- were some of these troops that had gone through, were they deployed to Bosnia as well, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I cannot say up to where they went. They stopped -- maybe some stopped at Knin, whatever the place, they passed us and some came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this officer that you talked about that expressed some surprise at the destruction, did he also express some shame that that had happened?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I want -- I cannot say if it was shame or -- but he -- when I talked to him, he was surprised to see that much destruction because when they did the attack the Serbs fled, you know, they all fled and it was a quick advance when they progressed and there were a lot more destruction when he came back than when they went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to move to a subject that was talked about in your statements concerning the observation posts, and I know that you weren't in the sector at the time, but I just want to ask you a few questions about what you learned about similar to what was asked on direct. Basically, Colonel, your job in the area was one of - and I say CanBat's job in the area - was one of observing and reporting; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say observing and reporting, can you just tell me what you mean by that just a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Okay. There were a cease-fire agreement established between the Croats and the Serbs, and the UN as a normal fashion under Chapter 6 of the UN Charter deployed troops into position between the belligerents and you are there to keep that buffer zone as free as much as possible either as part of the belligerents so we don't reignite the conflict. So that creates space for a negotiation to have a lasting peace settlement. So the aim of the mission was to occupy that zone and observe and report and we were doing a bit more than that, but if we saw something or somebody coming into the zone we are going to intercept them and say, Hey, you don't have any business here, then we're escorting them outside of the zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say observe and report, what were you reporting?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: If there were any activities like illegal crossing of the zone of separation, that's when -- we were in the normal operating mode before the offensive, if there were an infringement of that zone of separation, then we had to report that and then try to resolve that issue by convincing, by negotiation and persuasion, the party that was not following the cease-fire agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, let me ask you, are you familiar with this order that came from Zagreb called the order for active presence? And let me just bring it up and show it to you, it's 1D270002 to 1D270009. And if I can -- are you familiar with this document? If we can turn to the next page. This is a document that has written on the top there, Colonel, 24 July at 1400. And this was signed by General Alradan [phoen]. This is a document that came in after the events in Srebrenica, isn't it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, 24th of July, first of all, the 24th of July I was not in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you become aware of this document at all?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I don't have a recollection of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could just -- could I ask you a specific question and see if it jogs your recollection. If we could go to page 5 of 8, and in that phase 3 area of -- this is dealing with Sector South. Were you aware this order had been given at phase 3, ii when and where possible interpose between the warring parties in the Dinara mountain. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that there were problem in the east and they were -- fact they even consider to redeploy part of my battalion more to the east to help, they were looking at redeployment in Sector South to have more troops in the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this idea of interposing between the warring factions, was that a change in your mandate to observe and report?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: No. I mean we do observe and report by interposing ourselves in between. That is why we do deploy in the zone of separation in between, we interpose ourselves between the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But not engage in any degree of combat?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: No, because we were under chapter 6 and chapter 6 of the UN tells you that can only use force in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'll offer this cable into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D288 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now just to go into the events, and you had talked quite a bit about the reports that had come in to -- and that you had reviewed, albeit after you came back into the sector, and if we can just address the information you received concerning the 4th and the 5th, basically the 4th. If I can turn to P314, paragraph 1. Now, paragraph 1 of 314 notes that: "A warning from CEM ... CCUNPF at the 3rd of August 03, at 2200 hours indicates a possible Croatian offensive ..." Now, sorry sir.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware that that warning had come in?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I was told by my deputy when I came back that they had received that warning at 10.00 before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And was the warning that the Croats were going to attack the following morning?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: They didn't specify the specific time-frame, but they said that it was an imminent attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with this imminent attack, and I understand that you weren't there, Colonel, the CanBat 1 still had their soldiers out in the observation posts that we saw in P317, did they not?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is there some reason why with the imminent attack or you being informed of the imminent attack why the troops were not brought back to battalion headquarters in Rastevic?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Because that will defeat the purpose of our mission. Our mission is to, like I said, to make an interposition between the two belligerents and observe and report. So if we all return to camps, there's no -- we don't complete our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, a code red was declared at 0400 on the 4th, yet the CanBat 1 was still not taken out of those observations posts, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Code red means you stay in place, you don't travel if not necessary except on an emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you understood that during this time that looking at this particular attack on an international level, it was in the best interests of the Croatian army to use their best efforts not to hurt any UN employees; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a rather useless question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, it's always whatever the witness says about it. Of course that goes without saying. Let's not talk about the obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I won't belabour the point but there are a certain amount of facts that need to be brought out that can be discussed with this Chamber down the line, and I'm simply trying to lay those facts out. But if Your Honour accepts that as a given, then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever considered this Chamber to think that it was in the interests of the Croatian forces to inflict damage on the UN personnel there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would be in the interests, not what was done. I mean, we're talking about facts primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witnesses come and tell us what they have observed, what they have seen, what they have heard, and what the in the interests of A or B. At least I -- but let me just check ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept the conclusions that the Chamber has made on this score and I will just move to this next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note in Exhibit 311, if I can just quote it for you and get the proper page. This is 311, page 2 of 7, paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: You said page 2 of 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're going to bring it up on the screen, Colonel. It's a document that the Prosecution put into evidence. Excuse me, I apologise, 312, it's the follow-up. 312. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document that was provided to me has a different paragraph 20 than the document that has been admitted into evidence, which has none. As you note, there is no paragraph 20 there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although there are a few lines which follow the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those are different than the document that was disclosed as part of the 92 ter submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will quote what I have and we can clarify the matter, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it appears to me, Mr. Kehoe, that first of all the -- where in paragraph 19 the English says A, B, C, apparently the other version says 1, 2, 3. And then where in the B/C/S version there are four lines which form paragraph 20, by comparing the most obvious parts of that text it appears that, although not numbered, the next four lines in the English appear at first sight with all reservations I can make to present more or less a similar matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, using the document that's on the screen, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interrupt, I believe the English translation on e-court at the moment is the incorrect one and that is correct, in fact, what was tendered with the 92 ter submission is not the one that is on e-court so there has been another confusion. I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that everyone accepts the apologies. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So let me just read to you the document that I do believe was submitted, it notes that: "They," talking about the Croatian army, "demonstrated a great deal of precision in their shelling." Colonel, that was what you were told during the period of time after you came back and you were debriefed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it was that that led you to conclude, if I may, in your 1996 statement on page 3, that's P308, to conclude on page 3 paragraph -- the fourth full paragraph you note that -- you see that: "Also during Operation Storm," are you with me, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's page 3.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Five paragraphs down: "Also during Operation Storm ..." This is your 1996 statement, the first one.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is on the -- you see it on the screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You note it says: "Also during Operation Storm the Croatian army shelled three CanBat observation posts all located in the zone of separation. Two of these posts were under Charlie Company and one under Bravo Company. Fortunately, nobody was killed. Serbs were close to these OPs and in my understanding the Croats aimed their weapons against the Serbs. I wouldn't say that these UN posts were shelled deliberately, but rather due to the near proximity of the Serbs." Now, that's based on the conversations that you had with your subordinate staff members when you returned; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, there was an incident, sir, where the Croats went to the observation posts and attempted to get your soldiers to vacate those observation posts; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: In many instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you, if I can bring up 1D270033. As we're bringing this up, Colonel, this is a column that you wrote for -- let me see, the Sun Media -- the Ottawa Sun. If you can take a look at it. You can orient yourself on that, sir. And if we can go to the second page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first full paragraph: "Our rules of engagement ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Our rules of engagement permitted the use of force in protection only. The Croats were well aware of this fact and approached our isolated observation posts in groups of 20 to 40 soldiers in a non-threatening" manner. So it would be accurate to say, Colonel, that when the Croatian army went to these observation posts, they went up there and began a series of discussions with the individuals in those observation posts asking them to leave?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And after those negotiations they didn't -- they did, in fact, leave several of those observation posts, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, some were -- there were eight observation posts that were forced out by the Croats army to go to be sent to Zadar, and the eight others stayed in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the areas they were asking them to move out was an area that the HV offensive was moving through?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When they allowed these Canadian soldiers to leave, they allowed them to take their weapons and their vehicles and their equipment, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Not all of them. It varies from one place to the other. Some the -- they didn't have the choice to leave everything in place and some others they were able to bring that with them. It varies from one observation post to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me -- if I can move this article into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D289, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. D289 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can bring up 1D270037.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is an article from the Canadian Press, Colonel, back on August 8th. If we can blow that up on the front. And we're just going to that fourth insert down where your name is, do you see that, Colonel? And you are talking about the period of time after these individuals left the observation posts you note: "But the Canadians suffered no casualties and neither Serbs nor Croats aimed any hostile action at Canadians, said Lieutenant-Colonel Jacques Morneau, commander of CanBat 1." Is that accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you say that to the press?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I doubt that I said that aimed any hostile action at Canadians, because there had been a number of hostile actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, there were no casualties suffered by the CanBat forces, were there?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: There were no casualties because of the good work of the soldiers for four months with building up those observation posts with a lot of sand bags, because if there had not been at those defensive protection, there would have been casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then they were taken down to Zadar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: The one that were forced to evacuate the observation posts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a video --

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: But not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: The initial ones on the 4th, they were evacuated to Zadar, but then when the I will say the rules of the deception of coming close friendly and then invading the observation post was kind of bad. They would pass around and people were more alert and more resisting I will say the eviction of the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, was there individual --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we've just got to wait to catch up. Your Honour, before we move forward I will move this article into evidence. Your Honour, before I move on to this video if I can just move this article into evidence, 1D270033 -- excuse me, 0037. It's the article of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D290 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have an individual on your staff by the name of Jeff Agnew, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was my public affairs officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a video, and the video is -- begins at 1D270010.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the booths have transcripts of this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we follow the usual procedure that if it goes too quick that one of the interpreters checks whether what is on paper has been said and the other one has an opportunity to interpret. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a CBC news clip from 6 August 1995. If we can play this

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Of course, there are Canadians caught in this conflict. More than 750 Canadian peace keepers are serving in the region at bases and observation posts. Early on in the fighting Croatian forces took some Canadians from their posts and moved them just outside Krajina to Zadar where they remain tonight. Joining me tonight to talk about the situation is Jeff Agnew, commander of the Canadian forces in Croatia. Lieutenant-commander Agnew, what is the latest on the Canadians in Zadar? "Well, we have 43 soldiers who are in Zadar. They are currently staying in a Croatian camp, they are guests of the Croatians, they are free to move about. However, we are waiting now until the fighting ceases and we can make arrangements to take them back to their base camp in Rastevic. "There are reports today that some UN peacekeepers are being used as human shields by the Croats. You have no reason to believe that the Canadians are at any risk at Zadar. "No, not at all. In fact, once it was clear that we were going to abandon our observation posts they were most cordial, they escorted us out of the area, took the soldiers back to Zadar, they in fact stayed the night in a hotel. The only thing they are really concerned about is their continuing on with their offensive operations and you just don't need a number of stray soldiers moving about the field that no one knows about and so the Canadians will simply wait in Zadar until they have an opportunity to return back to Rastevic. "So how many Canadians are currently staffing outposts in the area? "Well, we have 43 soldiers who are in Zadar. They are currently staying in a Croatian camp, they guests of the Croatians, they are free to move about. However, we are waiting now until the fighting ceases and we can make arrangements to take them back to their base camp in Rastevic. "Lieutenant-commander Agnew, thanks so much for talking to us. "My pleasure."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel -- Colonel, the comments by Mr. Agnew, I'm not familiar with his rank at this point, but of Mr. Agnew an accurate assessment of what you were informed of the treatment of these individuals when they were taken to Zadar?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me turn your attention to -- excuse me, before I do that I would like to tender this video into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D291, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D291 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock. This is the usual time for a break. Could I get -- I don't know how much time you would further need and I would like to inquire with the other Defence counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have a very brief, Your Honour. If I could take the break right now I could just discuss it with my co-counsel I think we could finish very quickly if we took the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know that terms like very quickly, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would say no more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No more than ten minutes. Other Defence counsel. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may be some issues that I raise, but it would be no more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm looking at the clock. Ten minutes for Mr. Kehoe, until 1.00; ten minutes for Mr. Kay until ten minutes past 1.00; and then, Mr. Kuzmanovic, until 1.30 for you. Would that be a good schedule, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, based on what has come out so far I don't anticipate more than five minutes of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's ten minutes left for the Chamber. We would also discuss during the break how much time we would need. We will break until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any news on your position in relation to P319, the video of which we saw only a part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not hear of any other objections, therefore P319 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Is it possible, I was cut before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to come back to that where you were cut off and just let you follow in from there.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: If I may just, I mean, following the video I was asked a question. I said no but I did not have time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we were now talking about another video which was played earlier, that is the burned, damaged houses, where the Defence asked to look at the whole of the video to see whether there were any objections, but I take it that the video we saw just before the break that Mr. Kehoe will now move to that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I was going to take it off from the no. I'm going to ask you, Colonel, whether that was an accurate assessment -- Mr. Agnew's statements were an accurate assessment of what transpired. You said no mand I was going to give you the opportunity to explain.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Okay. I mean it was not accurate at all. What he has reflected there was a lack of information of what was exactly happening. On the 6th of August, first of all, Mr. Agnew was in Rastevic in the battalion camp and the individuals that we are talking about, they were in Zadar, so he had never had the contact with them to discuss how they were taking prisoners and how they were treated in Zadar itself. So he had no exposure or information about it. Personally on the 6th of August I went to Zadar and I talked to the soldiers, and following that also I did the -- if you go through the declaration of each of the individuals that was taken over, prisoners, it was not in a friendly manner, it was very threatening manner. Also in Zadar they had no freedom of movement. I mean, they were sequestrated. I mean they were well treated but there were no freedom of movement. So we were not abused in Zadar itself, but they had no freedom of movement. And also just to I will say that video-clip is very misleading on what really happened on the ground. The lieutenant-commander, the individual Mr. Agnew is a lieutenant-commander in the Canadian navy and I don't want to undermine the Canadian navy but they don't know the army staff as a proper army officer. So I will be cautious about the comments that that individual did pass on to the media on that specific day because it's not the reflection of what had been seen and what had been reported by the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just with that answer go to P314, paragraph 57. This is a portion of the report that the Prosecution put into evidence through you. And if you can read paragraph 57, this is a CanBat report on the sequence of events: "57 of our soldiers in Zadar were well treated, they were fed and housed by the Croats free of charge."

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I do agree like I just said a minute ago. They were well treated as normal prisoners, but they were not in a friendly manner like it was depicted in the video-clip for Mr. Agnew or lieutenant-commander Agnew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I believe I moved the video into evidence as D291.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you very much for your time and I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the video is concerned, Mr. Registrar, that is in evidence now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe it is at 291, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is correct, it is admitted as Exhibit D291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what my recollection tells me. Then Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I only have some brief questions for you, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay is -- Mr. Morneau, is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The matter I want to ask you about concerns the role of Croatian army liaison officers. Looking through your reports that have been exhibited to the Court we can see frequent references in those documents to Croatian army liaison officers with whom you had dealings. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at them for my part it seems like you were dealing with them on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: We had -- I had my own liaison officer that were on a daily basis in Zadar dealing with them. Personally I was not on the daily basis but on infrequent occasion I was going to Zadar to discuss with them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just to clarify matters, you had your own Canadian army liaison officer liaising with the Croatian army liaison officer; is that what you meant, to be clear?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: It is clear and it is very unusual I will say, if you allow me to explain that situation, an unusual situation because normally when you have a theatre of operation when you have belligerents, the interposition force will deal directly with the force deployed on the ground. So like my troops, the OPs, the company commanders will have the opportunity to go on both sides of the zone of separation to discuss with either the Croats commander, the brigade commander, the battalion, the company commanders, and the same thing on the Serb side. But in this instance the Croats army did restrict any contact of any UN soldiers to be in direct contact with the Croats whatever echelon that they had. They all had to go through a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and you've hit precisely on the matter I was going to ask you about. And we can see in relation to the dealings with the 43 Canadian soldiers who were subject to the control of the Croatian forces, that you were dealing with a Croatian army liaison officer in sorting out that problem. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, in a sense, yes. We had to go through the CALO in Zadar to negotiate the release of the 43 Canadian officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you said CALO, it's C-A-L-O, Croatian army liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to tidy up our record here. What rank were you dealing with the Croatian army liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Navy captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that Mr. Lukovic?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: One of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the names of the others?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Milojanic [phoen] or something like that. I will have to check the notes somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did they refer to Zagreb for various authorities or to deal with the problems that you were raising?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: No, they were dealing with Split, the headquarter in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Were you aware that they had a commander in Zagreb, a brigadier Prestina [phoen] who was in charge of the Croatian army liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Not that specific brigadier. My understanding they were reporting to the joint commanding officer, Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: Gotovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The number of Croatian army liaison officers that you were dealing with, are you able to help us?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: I mean, the other liaison office, so they were -- I would say the lead of that liaison office were the two navy captains that we just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: But there were other staff working for them. So I don't know the numbers what they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just leaving that point there as that's all I need ask. One other matter. In relation to the 43 Canadians who were detained, was that a matter that was raised at a political level, far higher up as between your state and the Croatian state so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES MORNEAU
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not raised through the Canadian political level as far as I know, but it was -- we were detach operational under command of the operational control of the UN, so it was a responsibility of the UN to do a political representation. So my superior was the sector commander in Knin who report to the force headquarter in Zagreb and then they were the representatives of the Secretary-General there that was I will say dealing with the political dimension. So it will have been in Zagreb that you will have that interface between the UN forces and the Croats political authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any -- I have no need to ask you any further matter about that. You've given a clear answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kuzmanovic, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Morneau?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Morneau, Mr. Kuzmanovic is Defence counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just mention something just before Mr. Kuzmanovic starts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Kuzmanovic inquired to the annexes to the particular document P318 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the five-page document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Five-page document which has 26 pages of annexes to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.
